Assignment 06 / Sculpting for Design

Essence in Subtraction

I explored growth and blooming by carving an abstract rose from floral foam.

Floral foam · Carving

I began with an idea of growth and allowed a rose-like form to emerge as I worked. Subtraction introduced a different kind of decision: a carved-away element cannot simply be put back.

01

Something growing from a block

The exercise called for an abstract form. I began without a fixed design, but wanted the piece to suggest growth or blooming. As I carved, that idea became an abstract rose with vine-like forms spreading out from the bud.

I enjoyed seeing my visualisation gradually take shape as I removed more material. The curled centre contrasts with the lower forms extending around it.

02

A form discovered through subtraction

I did not begin with a complete design. I used growth and blooming as a starting point, allowing the curled bud and spreading forms to develop as I carved.

My photographs show the same sculpture from several viewpoints. Turning it reveals the central spiral, surrounding openings, and the base connecting the curves into one form.

03

Working with floral foam

I found the foam pleasant to work with and enjoyed seeing my idea materialise. Each cut changed the shape I had available for the next decision.

I found subtraction more permanent than additive sculpting because I could not simply replace what I had removed. The finished rose records those decisions in the form left behind.

The original pages.

This shared submission documents the foam study on page 2 and the separate plaster carvings on pages 3–4.
